title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Power Plants | PT (US)
description: Liquid penetrant testing of stainless piping, HRSG welds, castings and hydro parts at US power plants: surface crack checks on nonmagnetic metal. Quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Power Plants: Dye Penetrant Inspection of Stainless, Alloy and Cast Parts
html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing (PT, or dye penetrant inspection) on stainless steel piping, nickel alloy and nonferrous components, castings and weld repairs at US power plants. PT finds cracks and laps that break the surface of any nonporous metal, magnetic or not. Technicians are mobilized to your plant and report to your inspector or engineer. Request a PT inspection quote with the component list, material and outage dates.

Where penetrant testing fits in a power plant

Magnetic particle inspection only works on iron-based steel, and a power plant has plenty of metal that is not. Austenitic stainless steel lines in feedwater heaters and sampling systems, nickel alloys in high-temperature service, copper-nickel condenser parts, aluminum bus enclosures and bronze valve trim cannot be magnetized. Penetrant testing is the surface method for all of these. The idea is simple: a low-viscosity liquid is drawn into a surface-breaking crack by capillary action, the excess is removed, and a developer pulls the trapped liquid back out so the crack shows as a line against the background.

PT does not see below the surface, it does not measure wall loss, and it will miss a crack that has been smeared closed by grinding or peening. For those questions the plant turns to ultrasonic testing for power plants, and for surface cracks on carbon steel to magnetic particle inspection for power plants, which is generally faster on ferritic parts. Our national penetrant testing page describes the method; this page covers power generation equipment.

Stainless steel piping and welds

Stainless lines in power plants appear in feedwater heater drains, auxiliary steam, sample and chemical feed systems, and in the high-purity circuits of combined cycle units. After a weld repair or modification, the finished weld and the heat-affected zone are commonly examined by PT. The concern is the type of crack stainless produces: hot cracking in the weld metal, and fatigue or stress corrosion cracking at the toe. Our job page penetrant testing of stainless steel goes through technique for these alloys in more detail.

One detail matters more on stainless and nickel alloys than anywhere else: contaminants in the penetrant materials. ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165 limit halogen and sulfur content in penetrants, cleaners and developers used on austenitic stainless steels, nickel alloys and titanium, because residues left behind can promote cracking in service. We use materials that carry batch certifications for those limits, keep them in our job documentation, and wipe and rinse the part thoroughly after the examination. Plants with stricter owner rules should send them with the request.

HRSGs, boilers and pressure part repairs

PT shows up in boiler and HRSG repairs wherever the base metal is nonmagnetic, or where the joint geometry makes magnetic particle work impractical: small-bore connections, stainless or alloy tube-to-header welds, and attemperator liners. In combined cycle plants, thermal cycling is a regular source of surface cracking on dissimilar metal welds, where a ferritic part is welded to an austenitic one. Because the transition falls across a magnetic and nonmagnetic boundary, PT is the usual surface method across the whole joint. Repairs on pressure parts are done under ASME Section I and the National Board Inspection Code (NBIC), and your authorized inspector decides which examination and acceptance level the repair needs.

Castings, turbine and hydro components

Valve bodies, pump casings, turbine nozzle boxes and other castings can have porosity, shrinkage and cracks that open to the surface. PT is widely used on cast stainless and alloy parts, and on machined surfaces of components made of nonferrous metal. The penetrant testing of castings page covers the rougher surface challenges of cast material. On hydro projects the same method is used on bronze and stainless wicket gate hardware, runner repairs on stainless overlay, and weld repairs on cavitation-eroded surfaces. Rotating parts supplied by an original equipment manufacturer are examined to that manufacturer's criteria when the owner says so.

Technique: penetrant type, dwell and temperature

Plant work is nearly always done with solvent-removable penetrant and solvent cleaner, because it can be applied to a part in place without a water supply or a wash station. Visible red dye is the default in the field. Where greater sensitivity is required, such as on a polished or machined surface, fluorescent penetrant and a black light in a darkened area can be used. Solvent-removable systems follow Article 6 procedure: clean, apply penetrant, allow the dwell time stated in the procedure, wipe the excess with a dry cloth, finish with a lightly dampened wipe, apply a thin film of nonaqueous developer and examine in the developing time.

Temperature limits are important. Article 6 normally allows examination of surfaces between roughly 40 and 125 degrees Fahrenheit; outside that range the procedure must be qualified, which is a common point on piping that is still warm or on an unheated winter outage. We state the surface temperature in the report. Cleaning is the other half of a good result: oil, scale or weld spatter that fills a crack prevents penetrant from entering, so we clean the surface with solvent and mechanical methods and avoid shot blasting, which can smear metal over a flaw. Our Article 6 explainer describes each step in order.

Dissimilar metal welds and post-examination cleaning

Dissimilar metal welds join a ferritic part, such as a chrome-moly header, to an austenitic one, such as a stainless attemperator line. They are among the more failure-prone joints in a heat recovery plant because the two metals expand at different rates. The fusion line on the ferritic side can be examined by magnetic particle, but the stainless side cannot, so a single PT examination across the whole joint keeps the record in one piece. We clean from the weld outward by at least the width set in the procedure and examine the weld metal, both fusion lines and the heat-affected zones.

When the examination is finished, the part is not done. Penetrant and developer residue must be removed before the system is closed or returned to service, particularly on stainless and nickel systems, where residual contaminants can matter. We wipe and flush with an approved solvent, remove any developer film, and record the cleaning in the report so the plant's chemistry and operations staff can see the work was closed. Where a joint will be welded again, the cleaning step also keeps penetrant out of the next weld pass, which can cause porosity.

Codes and acceptance

ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165 describe the method. Acceptance criteria come from the construction or repair code, such as ASME Section I or B31.1, from NBIC repair requirements, or from the owner's specification. For most welds, linear indications above a stated length are rejected and rounded indications are evaluated by size and spacing. We state the exact criteria used in every report. Where code and owner specification differ, the stricter requirement usually applies, but the decision rests with your authorized inspector or engineer.

What the report contains

  • Plant, unit, system and component identifiers matching your drawings
  • Procedure number and revision, and the governing code or specification
  • Penetrant, cleaner and developer type, with batch numbers and contaminant certifications where required
  • Surface preparation, dwell time, developing time and surface temperature
  • Technician name and qualification level
  • Each indication with location, length, orientation and accept or reject
  • Sketches or photographs showing coverage and any limitation

A Level II performs and interprets; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. Atlantis supplies data. It does not decide fitness for service or sign as authorized inspector.

What to send for a quote

  • Component list, drawings or weld maps with quantities
  • Base metal and filler, including any dissimilar joints
  • Contaminant limits required by your specification
  • Governing code, repair plan or acceptance criteria
  • Surface condition and temperature, and any coating
  • Access, scaffold, confined space and permit requirements
  • Outage dates, site badging or background check requirements and the site address

Planning around the outage

PT is slow compared with MT because the penetrant must dwell before it can be wiped, and the developer needs a few minutes, so a crew working a large number of welds needs a sensible sequence. Welders usually work ahead of the examiner, and rework means starting over. On stainless systems, plants also coordinate with chemistry staff on cleaner and solvent residue before the system is returned to service. Insulation, scaffold and rope or lift access are arranged by the plant, and our technicians arrive prepared for orientation, lockout and tagout and any screening your site requires.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, which is licensed under 10 CFR Part 34 or Agreement State rules. We do not hold 10 CFR 50 Appendix B qualification, so safety-related nuclear components are outside our work. We do not offer specialist techniques on this page, and we do not calculate remaining life or fitness for service.

Where we work in the US for power generation

  • Charlotte: Carolinas gas-fired units with stainless and alloy repairs.
  • Knoxville: Tennessee Valley hydro and fossil stations with bronze and stainless hardware.
  • Atlanta: Southeastern combined cycle HRSGs and their dissimilar metal welds.
  • Birmingham: Alabama plants and valve and casting suppliers.
  • Phoenix: desert peaking plants where cycling cracks alloy welds.
  • Chicago: Midwestern generation with older stainless auxiliary systems.
  • Pittsburgh: Ohio River Valley power and heavy cast parts shops.
  • Tampa: Florida units where coastal air attacks external stainless surfaces.

Training your own PT technicians

Plants that want in-house dye penetrant capability can start with PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training; see also power generation NDT training. The penetrant testing simulator gives trainees practice on dwell, cleaning and indication reading. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies, and we can write a written practice for your site. If you are unsure whether a part needs PT or MT, our comparison of MT and PT sets out the tradeoffs.

faq.q: Why use penetrant testing instead of magnetic particle at a power plant?
faq.a: Because MT only works on magnetic steel. Austenitic stainless, nickel alloys, bronze and aluminum cannot be magnetized, so PT is the surface method. PT is also used where parts are too small or irregular for a yoke.

faq.q: What contaminants matter when penetrant testing stainless steel?
faq.a: Halogens such as chlorides and fluorides, and sulfur, can promote cracking in austenitic stainless and nickel alloys. ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165 set limits, and we use batch-certified materials and clean the part afterward.

faq.q: Can you examine a pipe weld that is still warm?
faq.a: Only within the temperature range the procedure allows. The standard range is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside it the procedure has to be qualified, so we state the surface temperature and agree the plan with your inspector.

Penetrant testing cannot find cracks that do not break the surface, wall thinning or internal flaws. It can also miss tight cracks that are smeared closed by grinding, so we avoid blasting and heavy grinding before examination.

faq.q: Who decides whether an indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The acceptance criteria come from the construction or repair code, an NBIC repair plan or your specification. We report against the named criteria. Your authorized inspector or engineer makes the final call and any repair decision.

faq.q: Do you use fluorescent penetrant in the field?
faq.a: Sometimes. Visible dye with solvent removal is typical for plant work. Fluorescent penetrant gives higher sensitivity on smooth surfaces and needs a darkened area and black light, so we use it when the procedure and the site allow.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote PT on a plant repair?
faq.a: A component list or weld map, base and filler metal, contaminant limits, governing code and acceptance criteria, surface condition and temperature, access arrangements, outage dates, badging requirements and the site address.

faq.q: Do you inspect safety-related nuclear parts?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not hold 10 CFR 50 Appendix B qualification. Balance-of-plant scope can be considered where the owner's own program accepts our written practice and procedures.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be done on castings with rough surfaces?
faq.a: Yes, with care. Rough as-cast surfaces hold penetrant and can create background that hides indications, so we clean thoroughly, may use a different removal method, and evaluate indications in the context of the surface condition.
